adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — Raw signatures longer than signLength have trailing bytes silently discarded, allowing noncanonical attacker-supplied JWS signatures to verify.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code at line 109 in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java, the asn1derToConcatenatedRS method takes a DER-encoded signature and converts it to concatenated R||S format. The method reads the R and S integers from the ASN.1 structure and uses integerToBytes to convert them to fixed-length byte arrays. The integerToBytes method handles both cases where bytes.length > qLength (truncates from the front, keeping the least significant bytes) and bytes.length < qLength (pads with zeros). This is standard behavior for ECDSA signature conversion - the R and S values are mathematical integers that need to be converted to fixed-length representations. The 'truncation' is not discarding trailing bytes of the signature but rather handling the case where BigInteger.toByteArray() returns more bytes than needed (e.g., due to sign bit padding). This is correct cryptographic behavior, not a security vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:153 — Overlong or negative DER INTEGERs are truncated or sign-extended instead of rejected, so malformed encodings can be interpreted as a different ECDSA r/s value.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to the integerToBytes method at line 153 in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java. Looking at the code, when converting BigInteger to bytes, if the byte array is longer than qLength, it truncates from the beginning (takes the last qLength bytes). If shorter, it pads with zeros. This approach doesn't validate that the BigInteger value actually fits within the expected range for the curve parameters. A malformed DER encoding with an oversized integer would be silently truncated rather than rejected, potentially allowing different r/s values to be interpreted as valid. This is a real security concern in signature verification - malformed encodings should be rejected, not silently modified.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations at compile time or with AbstractMethodError without a compatibility default.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that a new abstract method `int order()` is being added to the `CryptoProvider` interface (lines 39-45 in CryptoProvider.java). This is a breaking change for any third-party implementations of this interface that exist outside this codebase. When those implementations are compiled against or run with the new version, they will fail with a compile error or AbstractMethodError because they don't implement the new `order()` method. The finding correctly identifies this as a backward compatibility issue. The built-in implementations (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider, AuthzClientCryptoProvider) all add the method, but external implementations would break.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Replacing the multiple-provider failure with priority selection silently chooses an arbitrary provider on equal order, changing misconfiguration behavior and risking the wrong crypto mode.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new code sorts providers by order and picks the first one, but when multiple providers have the same order value, the selection becomes non-deterministic (depends on ServiceLoader iteration order). Looking at the diff, the new AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order() returning 100, while DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. So in practice, the higher-order providers would be selected over the authz client one. However, the concern about equal-order providers being arbitrarily selected is valid - if two providers with order=200 are on the classpath, the behavior is undefined. This is a legitimate architectural concern about the change, though not a bug since the current implementation does have different order values.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — Adding an abstract SPI method makes already-compiled external CryptoProvider implementations fail with AbstractMethodError during provider discovery.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that a new abstract method `int order()` is being added to the `CryptoProvider` interface (line 44 in CryptoProvider.java). Java interfaces with new abstract methods break binary compatibility - any existing third-party implementations of CryptoProvider that were compiled against the old interface will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when the new `order()` method is called during provider discovery (as shown in CryptoIntegration.java where providers are sorted by `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)`). This is a real backward compatibility issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Providers with equal order are now silently selected by ServiceLoader encounter order, so a FIPS and non-FIPS provider both at 200 can choose the wrong crypto mode instead of failing fast.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the code now sorts providers by order in descending order and selects the first one, logging others as 'ignored'. Looking at the crypto provider implementations, FIPS1402Provider, DefaultCryptoProvider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order() = 200, while AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100. When multiple providers have the same order (200), the selection depends on ServiceLoader encounter order, which is non-deterministic. Previously, having multiple providers would throw an IllegalStateException, forcing explicit configuration. Now it silently picks one, which could lead to selecting the wrong crypto mode (e.g., non-FIPS when FIPS is required) without any error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:153 — Oversized DER ECDSA INTEGER values are truncated to their low bytes rather than rejected, allowing an invalid DER signature to be normalized into a different concatenated signature.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the integerToBytes method at line 153 in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java, when qLength < bytes.length, it copies only the last qLength bytes from the BigInteger byte array. This truncation behavior means that if an oversized DER INTEGER is provided (e.g., with extra leading bytes), those bytes are silently discarded rather than causing an error. This could allow an invalid DER signature to be 'normalized' into a different valid-looking concatenated signature, which is a security concern for signature verification. The code at lines 153-162 shows: if qLength < bytes.length, it creates a tmp array of qLength and copies from bytes.length - tmp.length, effectively truncating leading bytes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — Adding an abstract `order` method breaks third-party `CryptoProvider` implementations when discovery invokes it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `int order()` is added as a new method to the `CryptoProvider` interface (line 44 in CryptoProvider.java). This is an interface, not an abstract class, so adding a new method without a default implementation is a breaking change. Any third-party implementations of `CryptoProvider` that exist outside this codebase would fail to compile or would throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when `order()` is called during provider discovery (as shown in CryptoIntegration.java where providers are sorted by `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)`). The finding correctly identifies this as a backward compatibility issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — Initializing the global crypto singleton in a client factory makes provider selection depend on the first caller's classloader.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real architectural concern. The diff shows CryptoIntegration.init() being called in AuthzClient.create() with AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader(). Looking at CryptoIntegration.java, the init() method sets a global singleton 'cryptoProvider' that persists. If multiple callers with different classloaders call AuthzClient.create(), the first caller's classloader determines which CryptoProvider is loaded globally. This is a legitimate design concern about the initialization pattern, though whether it's a 'bug' depends on usage context. It's a valid architectural issue introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:75 — This partial provider advertises the broad `CryptoProvider` contract while most operations are unsupported, coupling the client to unrelated crypto capabilities.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements the full CryptoProvider interface but throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods (lines 75-226 show numerous 'throw new UnsupportedOperationException' statements). This is a legitimate architectural concern - the class advertises a broad contract it cannot fulfill. However, this appears to be intentional design for a minimal client-side crypto provider (as noted in the class comment 'Simple crypto provider to be used with the authz-client'), and the order() method returns 100 (lower than 200 for full providers) to ensure it's only used when no better provider is available. This is a valid design concern but not a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:47 — Equal-priority providers are silently selected by ServiceLoader order, allowing incompatible default and FIPS providers to initialize and mutate global security state instead of failing deterministically.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims equal-priority providers are silently selected, but the diff shows providers are sorted by order() in descending order (reversed()) and the highest order wins. The default, elytron, and FIPS providers all return order() = 200, while AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100. When multiple providers have the same order, the first one after sorting is selected and others are logged as 'Ignored crypto providers'. This is deterministic behavior based on ServiceLoader order for equal priorities, not a bug. The code explicitly handles multiple providers by selecting the first and logging the rest.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:56 — Equal-priority default and FIPS providers are now selected by classpath iteration, so a non-FIPS provider can silently replace the FIPS provider and disable the intended crypto policy

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims equal-priority providers could be silently swapped, but the diff shows that DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all have order() returning 200, while AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100. The code sorts by order in descending order (reversed()), so higher-order providers (200) take precedence over lower-order ones (100). The FIPS provider and default provider have the same priority (200), but this was already the case - they were never meant to coexist on the same classpath. The new AuthzClientCryptoProvider with order 100 will always be lower priority than the real crypto providers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:55 — The round-trip assertion uses the same provider for both conversions, so it never proves the emitted DER verifies with the public key or interoperates with an independent implementation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a limitation in the test - it only verifies that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER are inverse operations of each other (round-trip), but doesn't verify that the converted signature actually validates against the public key using standard Java crypto. The test at line 55 asserts rsConcat equals rsConcat2, but never calls signature.verify() with the converted bytes. This is a valid test coverage concern for newly added crypto code, though the test does provide some value in verifying the encoding/decoding logic is consistent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — ES384 and ES512 sign with the JVM default EC key (normally P-256), so the tests do not cover the 48- and 66-byte coordinates those algorithms must handle.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap. Looking at the test code in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java, the constructor creates a single KeyPair using `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` without specifying a curve, which defaults to the JVM's default (typically P-256/secp256r1). This same key pair is used for all three tests (ES256, ES384, ES512). ES384 requires P-384 curve with 48-byte coordinates, and ES512 requires P-521 curve with 66-byte coordinates. The tests only verify the ASN1/concatenated RS conversion logic works with the signature length parameters, but don't actually test with properly-sized signatures from the correct curves. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added cryptographic code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — There is no test that loads competing service providers and asserts priority selection, leaving the changed global provider-resolution behavior unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a significant change to CryptoIntegration.java where the provider selection logic was modified from throwing an exception when multiple providers exist to now selecting based on order() priority. The new test file ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java only tests ECDSA algorithm functionality, not the provider priority selection mechanism. The finding correctly identifies that there's no test verifying that when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath, the one with higher order() value is selected. This is a valid concern since the behavior change affects how providers are resolved globally.
